learningObjective: Reason about the memory and compute characteristics of FFT and related transforms as custom operators inside ML models.

canonicalClaims.claim: Cooley-Tukey FFT of length N has O(N log N) compute organized in log N butterfly stages; each stage reads/writes O(N) elements with small per-element flops, making large-N FFT bandwidth-bound on GPU.
conditions: N is a power of two for radix-2 FFT.
nonImplications: Does not imply FFT beats direct methods for small N.

canonicalClaims.claim: FFT-based convolution (via the convolution theorem) is competitive with direct convolution when the kernel is large enough; the FFT approach cost O((N+K) log(N+K)) crosses over direct O(N*K) as K grows.
conditions: Real-valued convolution can use R2C FFT to save ~2x.
Sequence length N is fixed by the workload.
nonImplications: Does not imply FFT-based convolution is exact; rounding differs from direct.

misconceptions.claim: FFT is bit-exact because Parseval preserves L2 norm.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Parseval is an identity in exact arithmetic; twiddle factors are irrational and round in FP.

misconceptions.claim: FFT is compute-bound because it has O(N log N) flops.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Per stage, flops per element are small and constant; memory bandwidth dominates.

misconceptions.claim: FFT-based convolution is always faster than direct convolution.
misconceptions.whyWrong: There is a kernel-size crossover; small kernels favor direct.

implementationFacts: cuFFT provides highly-tuned radix-N kernels for common N.
FlashFFTConv, S4/S5 SSMs, and Hyena rely on FFT-based long-range convolutions.
performanceScenarios: Real-input R2C FFT halves compute and memory vs full complex FFT.
